When Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth holds a press conference Tuesday, he will face a much different political landscape than the one he eked through in January 2025. That’s when he narrowly survived a 51-50 Senate confirmation. His support now appears to be substantially less.

   Rep. Thomas Massie (R., Ky.) introduced articles of impeachment against Hegseth on Monday. A vote could come later this week.

   Sen. Thom Tillis (R., N.C.) has called his vote to confirm Hegseth the “biggest regret of my career,” and other Republicans have signaled to the White House this week that Hegseth needs to go. 

   Hegseth is a fighter, and President Trump likes fighters, and so Hegseth is fighting.

   But twisting arms on Capitol Hill, like they did to get Hegseth confirmed last year, isn’t as easy with a shellshocked GOP that lost dozens of seats in last week’s election.

   Hegseth was one of the most ebullient cabinet members when Trump appointed Stephen Miller  to be chief of staff last week. For a moment, it made it look like Hegseth’s job was safe. But the ice beneath Hegseth was cracking over the weekend as Republicans sought to distance themselves. They aren’t showing that they would vote to impeach the defense secretary, but they are saying—publicly—that Trump has a decision to make.

Hegseth’s Impeachment Gives Wounded Hill GOP New Power
 
Plus, corporate America is lawyering up as it prepares for Democratic investigations, and Jeffries demands ‘dramatic change’ to immigration policy
 
 
EVELYN HOCKSTEIN/REUTERS
 

Good morning. When Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth holds a press conference Tuesday, he will face a much different political landscape than the one he eked through in January 2025. That’s when he narrowly survived a 51-50 Senate confirmation. His support now appears to be substantially less.

 

Rep. Thomas Massie (R., Ky.) introduced articles of impeachment against Hegseth on Monday. A vote could come later this week.

 

Sen. Thom Tillis (R., N.C.) has called his vote to confirm Hegseth the “biggest regret of my career,” and other Republicans have signaled to the White House this week that Hegseth needs to go. 

 

Hegseth is a fighter, and President Trump likes fighters, and so Hegseth is fighting.

 

But twisting arms on Capitol Hill, like they did to get Hegseth confirmed last year, isn’t as easy with a shellshocked GOP that lost dozens of seats in last week’s election.

 

They went from a 53-47 Senate majority to the possibility that they will hold only 44 seats next year. How can they get Hegseth’s budget and priorities through with that kind of deficit, not to mention the likely congressional oversight and investigations?

 

Hegseth was one of the most ebullient cabinet members when Trump appointed Stephen Miller to be chief of staff last week. For a moment, it made it look like Hegseth’s job was safe. But the ice beneath Hegseth was cracking over the weekend as Republicans sought to distance themselves. They aren’t showing that they would vote to impeach the defense secretary, but they are saying—publicly—that Trump has a decision to make.

 

They might have a decision to make first.

 

This is an edition of the Politics newsletter, bringing you an expert guide to what’s driving D.C. every day. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 
 
 

People and Policies I’m Watching

 

Pete Hegseth: The defense secretary will hold a press conference at 8 a.m. ET.

 

Senate Republicans: The GOP holds leadership elections to select a minority leader, whip, conference chair and other junior positions, following last week’s midterm elections.

 

Steve Scalise: The Louisiana lawmaker is running against Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio to lead House Republicans in the new Democratic-run Congress.

 

Trump’s Tuesday: The president is scheduled to hold several policy meetings.

What I’m Following

 
 
TOM WILLIAMS/CQ ROLL CALL/ZUMA PRESS
 

Corporate America is lawyering up ahead of an expected wave of Democratic investigations. After dominating Tuesday’s election, Democrats have dispatched letters telling companies they are targets and setting their deadline to produce records for Jan. 4, the first full day of the new Congress. Some of America’s largest businesses—from Amazon to Apple, Live Nation to Walmart—are among the first to feel the heat.

 

Top Democrat says Trump hasn’t reached out after the midterm elections. In a brief interview with the Journal outside a Verizon store in Washington, D.C., Hakeem Jeffries said that he was unaware of any conversations between the president and Democrats in recent days. Jeffries—set to be the next speaker of the House—said the House Democratic caucus will discuss immigration policy this week after Trump expressed openness to a deal. “We clearly need a dramatic change,” Jeffries said.

 

California voters reject an unprecedented tax on billionaires. The rejection of the ballot initiative, Proposition 40, ended a heated and expensive fight over what could have been the nation’s first modern tax on wealth. The outcome is a significant blow to supporters who had hoped to create a template for taxing wealth that could extend far beyond California.
